title: Junior-Senior Seminar
description: Analysis of a literary or cultural topic or problem through research and writing of two short and one long research paper for a minimum of 4,000 total words. Seminar follows EAS 190 ; related to the colloquium's subject.
prerequisites_raw: EAS 190 . Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement

title: Independent Study
description: Investigation of special topics through directed reading in translation. Paper required.

title: Topics in East Asian Religions
description: Selected topics in the religions of East Asia, e.g., Buddhism, Daoism, Shintô, Islam, shamanism.

title: Topics in East Asian Cultural Studies
description: Seminar, with topics varying from year to year. Research paper required.

title: Topics in East Asian Cinema
description: An examination of the possibilities of East Asian cinematic narrative. Possible topics: cinematic history; cinema in popular culture; comparisons with literary texts; major auteurs. Emphasis on technical as well as on thematic aspects. Includes readings in film theory.
prerequisites_raw: EAS 160

title: Independent Study
description: Directed research on topic determined in consultation with faculty member. A term paper or project is required.

title: Dissertation Research
description: Dissertation research for students who are advanced to doctoral candidacy.

title: Research in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
description: Individual research with Ecology and Evolutionary Biological faculty.

title: Research in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
description: Individual research with Ecology and Evolutionary Biological faculty.

title: Research in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
description: Individual research with Ecology and Evolutionary Biological faculty.

title: Seminar in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
description: Invited speakers, graduate students, and faculty present current research in ecology and evolutionary biology.

title: Graduate Tutorial in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
description: Advanced study in areas not represented by formal courses. May involve individual or small group study through reading, discussion, and composition.

title: Graduate Tutorial in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
description: Advanced study in areas not represented by formal courses. May involve individual or small group study through reading, discussion, and composition.

title: Graduate Tutorial in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
description: Advanced study in areas not represented by formal courses. May involve individual or small group study through reading, discussion, and composition.

title: Writing Grant Proposals
description: Provides students with hands-on experience writing proposals in the research areas of ecology, evolution, or physiology.

title: Special Topics in Ecology
description: Survey of special topics in Ecology.

title: Quantitative Methods in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
description: Statistics for ecologists and evolutionary biologists. Emphasis on specific applications and underlying assumptions rather than on methods of calculation. Topics include experimental design, parametric and nonparametric methods, analysis of variance and covariance, and multiple regression.
prerequisites_raw: Completion of at least one quarter of statistics including regression and analysis of variance

title: Foundations of Physiology
description: Physical and functional principles common to many living forms. Course forms a basis for subsequent specialization in any of the subdisciplines of physiology. Course offered in even years.

title: Co-Management Land Practices
description: Focuses on ethical co-management and collaborative land stewardship across diverse communities and governance structures. Students learn justice-oriented collaboration in practice through case studies and consultation with multiple partners.

title: Topics in Ecology
description: Weekly discussion of current topics in ecology at the graduate level.

title: Physiological Plant Ecology Lab
description: Provides a summary of information on plant organismal biology, comparative and ecological physiology, and functional ecology. Offered every other fall.

title: Topics in Microbial Ecology
description: Weekly discussion of current topics in ecology, biogeochemistry, evolution, and physiology of microbial organisms.

title: Communication Skills for Environmental Scholars
description: Students learn to communicate with non-specialist audiences about climate and environmental issues. Hands-on activities build technical, presentation, and contextual skills required for effective communication across a range of media types and careers.

title: The Physiology of Human Nutrition
description: Examines the biochemical basis of energy metabolism, physiological processes, indigestion and uptake, and the biochemical transformation of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins in the human body. The emphasis is on expanding the students' understanding of physiology.

title: Experimental Evolution
description: Explores experimental evolution, which is now a well-established part of evolutionary biology. With the advent of genomics, it is now one of the most powerful tools for studying the genetic foundations of biology.
prerequisites_raw: BIO SCI E106

title: Human Dimensions in Conservation and Restoration
description: The non-human “environment” we know today is the result of past social, political, scientific, and economic forces. Examines the forces that drove environmental conservation efforts, which often sought progress at the expense of local cultures.

title: Marine Conservation Ecology
description: Theory-based seminar tackles pressing issues in marine ecology, conservation, and restoration. Focuses on the science of marine ecosystems, resources and tools for their conservation, and management and the socioeconomic and policy dimensions.

title: Chemical Ecology
description: An introduction to the unspoken chemical language of nature. Emphasis on interactions between insects, plants, and microbes including plant defense, pollination, and microbial warfare.

title: Animal Locomotion
description: The physiology, biomechanics, and neuroscience that determines how animals propel themselves and navigate through the world. Considers the principles that govern the walking, running, flying, and swimming of animals, including exercising humans.
prerequisites_raw: Recommended: BIO SCI E109 or an introductory understanding of physiology

title: Comparative Animal Physiology
description: Maintenance aspects of physiology: water balance; feeding and digestion; metabolism; respiration and circulation.

title: Seminar in Ecology and Evolution Education
description: Weekly discussion of teaching techniques and challenges that are specific to courses in ecology and evolutionary biology. Emphasis will be on using evidence-based pedagogy techniques. There will be a combination of readings, group discussions and speakers.

title: Behavioral Endocrinology
description: Comparative examination of the major hormone systems that regulate behavior across animals. Emphasizes the reciprocating nature of hormone-behavior interactions and seeks to understand how natural selection drives the evolution of hormone structure and function.

title: Functional and Structural Evolutionary Genomics
description: Function and organization of genomes analyzed from an evolutionary perspective. Review of some of the most recent experimental approaches in genome analysis and comparative genomics. Relevant software to analyze DNA and expression data is used.

title: Advanced Quantitative Methods
description: Covers advanced analytical techniques used by conservation biologists. Methods include generalized linear models, community analysis using multivariate analyses, analysis of spatial/GIS data using R, time-series analysis, and meta-analysis.
prerequisites_raw: Recommended: ECO EVO 207

title: Professional Workshop
description: Identify and attend professional or technical skill workshops to gain professional knowledge and certifications related to conservation and restoration science.

title: Conservation Biology
description: Explores concepts in ecology with potential for conserving biological diversity. Identifies creative applications of ecological research that mitigate impacts of rapid human population growth and habitat destruction on biodiversity.

title: Restoration Ecology
description: Study of principles and practices that help recover degraded ecosystems including restoration in different ecological systems, restoration motives and intensities, implementation and monitoring, and scope and success of case studies.

title: Field Methods in Restoration
description: Laboratory experience performing field methods that help recover degraded ecosystems in different ecological systems. Emphasis on the plant community composition, soil, irrigation, maintenance, and monitoring of a project.

title: Science Communication
description: Develops students' abilities to convey information related to conservation and restoration in a way that has broad appeal and/or effective messaging for non-scientific audiences by assessing the audience, developing effective storytelling, and deploying a persuasive information campaign.

title: Technical Writing
description: Practice developing key documents for restoration projects including a response to a request for proposal (RFP), a restoration project plan, and a monitoring and maintenance plan.

title: Project Management
description: Discover the planning, design, implementation, and aftercare phases of managing a conservation or restoration project. Students will project cost, manage risk, analyze sites, evaluate and review projects, and become familiar with common permitting and consultation requirements.

title: GIS for Environmental Science
description: Introduction to the fundamental principles of GIS. Topics include cartography, creating/editing GIS data, georeferencing, map projections, geospatial analysis, spatial statistics, and development of GIS models. Focuses on theory and practice.

title: Advanced GIS for Environmental Science
description: Introduces the advance functions of Geographic Information Systems (GIS), including hic principles, and explores database mapping, computer-assisted analysis of spatial data, computer-aided map design, and the production of computer-generated maps.

title: Marine Research and Conservation Methods
description: Field-based introduction to marine ecology and conservation management through the study of the ecology, resource management, and conservation of marine habitats and species, and the use of a variety of marine field research methods.

title: Wildlife Ecology and Sampling
description: Field-based introduction to wildlife management through the study of the ecology, physiology, population biology management, and conservation of vertebrate wildlife species, and the use of a variety of different wildlife sampling techniques.

title: Environmental Education and Outreach
description: Prepares students to develop tailored education programs for conservation and restoration projects. Students engage in activities that foster innovative approaches and solutions to different education and outreach needs for conservation and restoration projects.

title: Evolution and Conservation
description: Examines evolution applications to conservation biology in three parts: processes of evolution within populations, conservation of species, and assessing evolutionary responses to environmental change.

title: Site Development
description: Students learn about plan review and the permitting processes as they relate to site development. Explores how a site is developed from application to building permits, and all the steps in between.

title: Fundamentals of Informatics for Biologists
description: Students learn the fundamentals of bioinformatics and the unix operating system.

title: Advanced Informatics for Biologists
description: Students learn advanced informatics including the analysis of: Poolseq, RNAseq, ATACseq, and ChiPseq datasets using programs such as bwa, tophat, cufflinks, DEseq, Trinity, Agustus, etc., in a unix high-performance computing environment. Statistical tests carried out and publication quality.
prerequisites_raw: ECO EVO 282 with a minimum grade of B-

title: MCRS Capstone
description: Apply knowledge and skills in a practical professional setting, working with practitioners to identify a conservation or management problem and then to plan, implement, and evaluate a solution.

title: Introduction to Economics
description: An analysis of the problems society faces in organizing itself to provide goods and services. How decisions of government, business, and the individual relate to current economic problems such as unemployment, inflation, poverty, and environmental pollution.

title: The Internet and Public Policy
description: How the Internet works. Current public policy issues concerning the Internet. Introductory economics. Communications law. Interactions between information technology, economics, and law. Case studies about Internet and communications policy.

title: Federal Reserve: Past, Present, and Future
description: Studies central banking in the United States from colonial times to the present. Focuses on the past, present, and future of the Federal Reserve and precursors to that system, which was established in 1913.

title: Global Economy
description: Acquaints students with the fundamental patterns of the global economy. Emphasizes the historical roots and political implications of economic choices.

title: Probability and Statistics for Economics
description: Introduces basic probability and statistics for econometrics. Knowing and understanding the details of statistics, statistical test, and conclusions about the test results. Problem sets provide practical experience on actual economic data using statistical packages.
prerequisites_raw: MATH 2A or AP Calculus AB with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus AB Subscore with a minimum score of 3 and ( MATH 2B or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 4)

title: Probability and Statistics in Economics I
description: An introduction to probability, statistics, and econometrics. Emphasis on a thorough understanding of the probabilistic basis of statistical inference. Examples from economics.
prerequisites_raw: MATH 2A or AP Calculus AB with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus AB Subscore with a minimum score of 3 and ( MATH 2B or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 4)

title: Probability and Statistics in Economics II
description: An introduction to probability, statistics, and econometrics. Emphasis on a thorough understanding of the probabilistic basis of statistical inference. Examples from economics.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 15A

title: An Economic Approach to Religion
description: Introduction to how basic economic concepts such as demand, supply, consumption, production, competition, free-riding, innovation, regulation, and rent-seeking can be applied to understand observed religious behavior.

title: Basic Economics I
description: The fundamentals of microeconomics. The behavior of firms and consumers: markets, supply/demand, utility maximization, resource allocation, and efficiency.

title: Basic Economics II
description: The fundamentals of macroeconomics. Government behavior: monetary and fiscal policy, inflation, and unemployment. Effective fall 2006, the content of Economics 20B is macroeconomics. This course cannot be taken to repeat Economics 20B taken prior to fall 2006.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 20A or AP Economics Micro with a minimum score of 4) or ECON 13 or ECON 23

title: Basic Economics for Engineers
description: The fundamentals of microeconomics. The behavior of firms and of consumers: markets, supply/demand, utility maximization, resource allocation, and efficiency.

title: The Economics of Accounting Decisions
description: Introduction to accounting concepts and principles, including the accounting model and accounting style, transaction analysis, and preparation of financial statements. An analysis of the similarities and differences between accounting and economic concepts (e.g., value, profits).
prerequisites_raw: ECON 20A

title: Learning Economics Through Sports
description: Introduces students to a selection of research topics in economics and other social sciences, using sports as laboratories and as sources of exceptionally-detailed data. Topics include labor markets, psychological biases and social forces, the adoption of innovations.

title: Intermediate Economics I
description: Determinants of supply and demand; operation of competitive and monopolistic markets; imperfections of the market system, explanations of unemployment, inflation, recessions; public policy for macroeconomic problems.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 20A or AP Economics Micro with a minimum score of 4) and ( ECON 20B or AP Economics Macro with a minimum score of 4) and ( MATH 2A or AP Calculus AB with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus AB Subscore with a minimum score of 4) and ( MATH 2B or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 4)

title: Intermediate Economic II
description: Determinants of supply and demand; operation of competitive and monopolistic markets; imperfections of the market system, explanations of unemployment, inflation, recessions; public policy for macroeconomic problems.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 100A or ECON 105A

title: Intermediate Economics III
description: Determinants of supply and demand; operation of competitive and monopolistic markets; imperfections of the market system, explanations of unemployment, inflation, recessions; public policy for macroeconomic problems.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 100B or ECON 105B

title: Intermediate Quantitative Economics I
description: An advanced and mathematical version of ECON 100A for students in the Quantitative Economics major.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 20A or AP Economics Micro with a minimum score of 4) and ( ECON 20B or AP Economics Macro with a minimum score of 4) and ( MATH 2A or AP Calculus AB with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus AB Subscore with a minimum score of 4) and ( MATH 2B or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 4) and MATH 3A

title: Intermediate Quantitative Economics II
description: An advanced and mathematical version of ECON 100B for students in the Quantitative Economics major.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 105A

title: Intermediate Quantitative Economics III
description: An advanced and mathematical version of ECON 100C for students in the Quantitative Economics major.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 105B

title: Economics of Asymmetric Information
description: Focuses on the effects of asymmetric information in the markets for traditional economic goods and resources, such as labor, insurance, used cars, credit, and in auctions and bargaining problems. Prerequisite:
prerequisites_raw: ECON 100A or ECON 105A

title: Game Theory of Human Cooperation and Morality
description: Teaches how game theory is used to understand human cooperation and morality. Covers basic game-theoretic concepts and analysis, how they illuminate what it means to be moral, and how prosocial human dispositions evolved.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 15 or ECON 15B or STATS 120B or MATH 130B ) and ( ECON 100A or ECON 105A )

title: Behaviorial Economics
description: Studies the behavioral and psychological biases in economics settings. Both individual decisions and games are discussed.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 20A or AP Economics Micro with a minimum score of 4) and ( ECON 20B or AP Economics Macro with a minimum score of 4)

title: Game Theory
description: Extensive form games with perfect information and coalitional games. The key solution concepts are Nash Equilibrium, Backward Induction, and the Core. Substantive examples include public good production, oligopoly, electoral competition, auctions, holdup, market entry, and voting.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 15 or ECON 15B or STATS 120B or MATH 130B ) and ( ECON 100A or ECON 105A )

title: Applied Econometrics I
description: Introduction to econometrics emphasizing practical applications in microeconomics and macroeconomics.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 100A or ECON 105A and ( ECON 15A or ECON 15B or ECON 15 or MATH 130B or MATH 133A or STATS 120C )

title: Applied Econometrics II
description: Introduction to econometrics emphasizing practical applications in microeconomics and macroeconomics.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 122A

title: Data Analysis Writing
description: Research writing course in econometrics focusing on individual research projects. Students employ econometric analysis to address an economic question in a 20-page paper and present their findings to the class in a short presentation.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 122A and ECON 122B . Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement

title: Econometrics I
description: Specification, estimation, and testing of econometric models. Applications in various areas of microeconomics and macroeconomics.
prerequisites_raw: ( MATH 2A or AP Calculus AB with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus AB Subscore with a minimum score of 4 or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 3) and ( MATH 2B or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 4) and MATH 3A and ( STATS 120C or MATH 130C ) and ( ECON 100A and ECON 100B and ECON 100C ) or ( ECON 105A and ECON 105B and ECON 105C )

title: Econometrics II
description: Specification, estimation, and testing of econometric models. Applications in various areas of microeconomics and macroeconomics.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 123A

title: Econometrics III
description: Seminar course in which students do an original econometric research project.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 123B . Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement

title: Business Forecasting
description: Students learn how to produce forecasts of the behavior of economic (and other) variables. The techniques examined are linear regression, nonlinear regression, and nonparametric kernel regression; AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA, and Box-Jenkins.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 122A

title: Computational Macroeconomics
description: Introduction to the computational methods for studying economic growth and the business cycle. Students learn how to write computer programs to simulate macroeconomic models, download and manage data from internet resources, and to do basic statistics.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 100C or ECON 105C ) and ( ECON 122A or ECON 123A )

title: Experimental Economics
description: Learn what constitutes proper experimental design and what laboratory experiments teach us about human behavior and the economy. Students participate in a sample experiment, evaluate the results, and discuss experiment design and larger issues. Formerly ECON 117.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 15 or ECON 15B ) and ECON 100B

title: The Economics of Opportunity
description: Examines factors that allow individuals to improve their economic situation regardless of their family’s economic circumstances during childhood. Covers various topics including neighborhoods, housing, education, healthcare, labor markets, and the criminal justice system.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 122A or ECON 123A ) and ( ECON 100A or ECON 105A ) and ( ECON 100B or ECON 105B ) and ( ECON 100C or ECON 105C ). Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement

title: Machine Learning for Economists
description: Develops the theory and computation of recent methods at the intersection of econometrics and machine learning as used in economics and business. Building on intermediate econometrics, it introduces causal random forests, double machine learning, and neural networks.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 123A

title: Special Topics in Quantitative Methods
description: Studies in selected areas of Quantitative Methods. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
prerequisites_raw: Prerequisites vary

title: The Economics of Risk and Uncertainty
description: The theory of insurance and joint-ownership of risky enterprises; optimal procedures for the allocation of uncertain payoffs.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 15 or ECON 15B or MATH 130B or STATS 120B ) and ( ECON 100B or ECON 105B )

title: Introduction to Financial Investments
description: Modern theories of investment and their application to the study of financial markets. The relation between risk and return, diversification, asset pricing, efficient markets hypothesis, and the market valuation of stocks, bonds, options, and futures.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 122A or ECON 123A ) and ( ECON 100A and ECON 100B and ECON 100C ) or ( ECON 105A and ECON 105B and ECON 105C ) or ( MATH 130A and STATS 120A and STATS 120B and STATS 120C ) or MATH 130B or MATH 133A

title: Markets and Networks
description: Introduction into network effects in economic settings, such as auctions, markets, and bargaining. Networks are also important in information diffusion, aggregation, and search. Some applications refer to traffic and epidemics.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 100A or ECON 105A

title: Corporate Finance
description: Provides an overview of the modern theory and practice of corporate finance and focuses on two fundamental financial decisions; investment as well as financing. Beginning with discounted cash flow analysis, basic theory will be applied to the valuation of stocks.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 100A and ECON 100B and ECON 100C ) or ( ECON 105A and ECON 105B and ECON 105C ) and ( ECON 15 or ECON 15B or MATH 130B or STATS 120B )

title: Corporate Finance II
description: Advanced material in corporate finance. How to value companies, debt and equity financing, capital structure, IPOs, venture capital, private equity, and mergers and acquisitions. Applies knowledge through cases and real-life examples.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 134A or MGMT 109

title: Mathematics of Finance
description: After reviewing tools from probability, statistics, and elementary differential and partial differential equations, concepts such as hedging, arbitrage, Puts, Calls, the design of portfolios, the derivation and solution of the Blac-Scholes, and other equations are discussed.
prerequisites_raw: MATH 3A

title: Financial Markets and the Macroeconomy
description: Students are required to write a paper on a research question related to financial markets and their interactions with the macroeconomic and political environment.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 122A or ECON 123A . Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement

title: Special Topics in Financial Economics
description: Studies in selected areas of Financial Economics. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
prerequisites_raw: MATH 2A or AP Calculus AB with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 4 and ( MATH 2B or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 4). Prerequisites vary

title: Managerial Economics
description: A collection of concepts and methods for effective decision making. Explores how the tools of microeconomics, including game theory and industrial organization theory, can be used to make better managerial decisions, particularly those involving allocation of resources within firms.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 100A and ECON 100B ) or ( ECON 105A and ECON 105B )

title: Health Economics
description: Builds off of economic theory to explore topics in health economics including health care demand, health insurance markets, the supply of health care, and examine health care policy.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 100B or ECON 105B

title: Public Economics and Development
description: Covers three topics of great relevance to governments in low-income countries: education, social insurance, and tax evasion. Through the lens of these topics, the basic questions of Public Economics, using theory and empirical evidence, are addressed.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 122A or ECON 123A

title: Industrial Organization I
description: The theory of market structure. Imperfect markets, government policies, and industry performance.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 15 or ECON 15B or STATS 120B or MATH 130B ) and ( ECON 100A and ECON 100B ) or ( ECON 105A and ECON 105B )

title: Industrial Organization III
description: Research in industrial organization. Imperfect competition, antitrust, and regulation.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 100A and ECON 100B ) or ( ECON 105A and ECON 105B ). Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement

title: Urban Economics I
description: Why cities exist, economics of urban land-use, housing demand and tenure choice, traffic congestion.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 20A or AP Economics Micro with a minimum score of 4) and ( ECON 20B or AP Economics Macro with a minimum score of 4). Recommended: ECON 100A

title: Urban Economics II
description: Housing policy analysis, urban public goods and services, crime, pollution, urban amenities.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 20A or AP Economics Micro with a minimum score of 4) and ( ECON 20B or AP Economics Macro with a minimum score of 4). Recommended: ECON 100A

title: Economics of the Environment
description: Surveys economic aspects of natural resources, pollution, population, and the environment. Examines the causes of pollution; analysis of public policies regarding these problems. Emphasis on microeconomic aspects of environmental problems.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 100A or ECON 105A

title: Economics of the Environment II
description: Applications of tools covered in ECON 145E to topics in environmental economics. Emphasis on independent research papers. Syllabus and classes include writing technique and use cutting-edge research papers as a base for developing effective reading, writing, and research skills.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 15A or STATS 120A or MATH 130A ) and ( ECON 15B or STATS 120B or MATH 130B ) and ( ECON 122A or ECON 123A ) and ( ECON 100A or ECON 105A ) and ( ECON 100B or ECON 105B ) and ( ECON 100C or ECON 105C ). Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement

title: Economics of Law
description: Examination of several economic concepts which are useful in understanding legal rules: externalities, the assignment of property rights, and Coase's theorem. Examples are drawn from the fields of pollution control, no-fault insurance, medical malpractice, and product liability.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 100A or ECON 105A ) and ( ECON 100B or ECON 105B )

title: Illegal Economics
description: How illegal firms function in illegal markets, why individuals participate in these groups and markets, and what federal, state, and local governments do to disrupt organized illegal activity.

title: Economics of Criminal Justice
description: Provides an introduction to the economics of crime literature.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 122A or ECON 123A

title: Conflict and Economics
description: Applies the tools of economics to study the causes and consequences of violent conflict (e.g., wars between nations, civil wars, and crime) and more refined forms of conflict (e.g., lobbying and litigation).
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 100A or ECON 105A ) and ( ECON 100B or ECON 105B )

title: Economics of Strategy
description: Uses tools of economics, game theory in particular, to develop an understanding of business decision-making. Deals with questions such as how the firm decides what kind of business to be in, how large should it be, and others.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 100A and ECON 100B ) or ( ECON 105A and ECON 105B )

title: Business Decisions
description: Surveys normative and descriptive models of decision-making behavior, with an emphasis on organizational and policy contexts. Topics include rational choice theory, biases and heuristics, framing effects, and overconfidence. Management fads, panics, and herd behavior are also discussed.
prerequisites_raw: ( ANTHRO 10A and ANTHRO 10B and ANTHRO 10C ) or ( SOCIOL 10A and SOCIOL 10B and SOCIOL 10C ) or ( SOC SCI 10A and SOC SCI 10B and SOC SCI 10C ) or ( MATH 2A and MATH 2B and ( STATS 7 or MGMT 7 ) or ( STATS 120A and STATS 120B and STATS 120C ) or ( ECON 15 or ECON 15B or MATH 130B )

title: Special Topics in Economics of Public and Private Organizations
description: Studies in selected areas of Economics of Public and Private Organizations. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

title: Labor Economics and Human Resources I
description: Labor demand, labor supply, human capital, personnel economics, and other topics.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 15 or ECON 15B or STATS 120B or MATH 130B ) and ( ECON 100A and ECON 100B ) or ( ECON 105A and ECON 105B )

title: Labor Economics and Human Resources II
description: Labor market discrimination, compensating wage differentials, immigration, and other topics.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 151A

title: Economic Anthropology
description: Economic systems in comparative perspective: production, distribution, and consumption in market and non-market societies; agricultural development in the third world.
prerequisites_raw: One course in general science, anthropology, economics, geography, or sociology

title: Political Institutions, Legal Systems, and Economic Development
description: Studies a variety of empirical papers analyzing how institutions affect economic development. The topics include cross-country studies of institutions as well as narrower topics such as corruption, regulation of entry, political connections, and pork barrel politics.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 100A or ECON 105A ) and ( ECON 100B or ECON 105B ) and ( ECON 100C or ECON 105C ) and ( ECON 122A or ECON 123A ). Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement

title: Voting and Political Manipulation
description: Introduction to social choice and cooperative games. Topics include majority rule, types of voting methods, apportionment and proportional representation, agenda manipulation, coalition formation, voting power, political consequences of electoral laws.

title: Current Issues in Political Economy
description: Political economy seeks explanations that combine insights from both economics and politics. Topics include the interaction of government and markets, the causes of the Great Recession, and the sources of income and wealth inequality.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 20A or AP Economics Micro with a minimum score of 4) or ( ECON 20B or AP Economics Macro with a minimum score of 4) or ECON 13 or INTL ST 13

title: Economic Development
description: Considers the process of economic development across the globe and why some countries are rich and others poor. Discusses the major problems facing developing countries, such as population growth, education, capital formation, environmental protection, and international trade.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 20A or AP Economics Micro with a minimum score of 4) and ( ECON 20B or AP Economics Macro with a minimum score of 4)

title: Money and Banking
description: Basic elements of money and banking: institutional features and economics of financial markets and, in particular, the U.S. banking system; determinants of interest rates; the Federal Reserve and its role in money supply; effects of money on output and inflation.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 100A and ECON 100B ) or ( ECON 105A and ECON 105B ) and ( ECON 100C or ECON 105C )

title: International Money
description: Open economy macroeconomics and determination of exchange rates. Asset-market approach to the balance of payments. Internal and external balance in the economy. Macroeconomic policies under fixed and floating exchange rates. The international monetary system and institutions.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 100A and ECON 100B ) or ( ECON 105A and ECON 105B ) and ( ECON 100C or ECON 105C )

title: Advanced Money and Banking
description: Studies business cycles in the United States during the last century. The first portion of the course reviews the theoretical models employed to study economic fluctuations and empirical methods used to measure fluctuations.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 161A and ( ECON 100C or ECON 105C )

title: Poverty, Growth, and Development
description: Examines India as a case study for each of the topics studied: growth experience of India along with its poverty eradication record, aspects of poverty, and the policies that have been undertaken to tackle poverty.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 15 or ECON 15B or STATS 120B ) and ( ECON 100A and ECON 100B and ECON 100C ) or ( ECON 105A and ECON 105B and ECON 105C )

title: Poverty and Inequality
description: Examines the measurement, causes, consequences, and correlates of poverty and inequality in the United States. Topics include the roles of public policy responses through income taxes, transfers, and direct labor-market interventions, family structure and neighborhoods.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 15 or ECON 15B or STATS 120B or MATH 130B ) and ( ECON 100A or ECON 105A )

title: The Industrial Revolution in Western Europe
description: How do economists explain the process of economic development during the past three centuries? Has the process of industrialization affected living standards? Focusing on these questions, students learn how to apply economic theory and quantitative methods.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 100C or ECON 105C . Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement

title: American Economic History from Colonization to the Present
description: Examines how the American economy evolved from colonization to the post-war era. Topics include relations with foreign countries, the emergence of manufacturing and big business, railroads, slavery, war, the Great Depression, the rise of fiscal and monetary policies.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 20A or AP Economics Micro with a minimum score of 4) and ( ECON 20B or AP Economics Macro with a minimum score of 4)

title: Economics of International Business
description: Students learn to understand and analyze the principal economic issues in the international business arena. Covers topics such as trade theory, foreign direct investment, foreign exchange market, and strategy of international business.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 100C (may be taken concurrently) or ECON 105C (may be taken concurrently)

title: Development Economics
description: Uses theory and empirics to understand the economies of low- and middle-income countries. Explores the concept, determinants, and consequences of economic growth, drawing on historical and cross-country evidence. Topics include poverty, inequality, agriculture, demography, and strategies of risk management.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 122A or ECON 123A ) and ( ECON 100A or ECON 105A ) and ( ECON 100B or ECON 105B ) and ( ECON 100C or ECON 105C )

title: International Trade and Commercial Policy
description: Determination of trade flows and the relative prices. Gains from trade, the terms of trade, and income distribution. Imperfect competition and international trade. The effect of tariffs, export subsidies, and import quotas. The effects of free and restricted trade.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 100A or ECON 105A

title: Special Topics in Development Economics
description: Studies in selected areas of Development Economics. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
prerequisites_raw: Prerequisites vary

title: Senior Thesis
description: Students work with faculty to complete their honors thesis.

title: Economics Honors Colloquium II
description: Colloquium required for honors students in Economics, Quantitative Economics, and Business Economics. Introduces students to independent research and helps students plan a research program. Students complete their thesis.
prerequisites_raw: ECON H190A . Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement

title: Economics Honors Colloquium I
description: Colloquium required for honors students in economics, quantitative economics, and business economics. Introduces students to independent research. Helps students plan a research program. Prepares students for thesis writing.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 122A or ECON 123A . Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement

title: Independent Study
description: Independent research with Economics faculty.

title: Graduate Colloquium for Economics I
description: Weekly reports and colloquia by faculty, students, and visitors. Supplemented by class discussion of these presentations and other material on current research methodology.

title: Graduate Colloquium for Economics II
description: Weekly reports and colloquia by faculty, students, and visitors. Supplemented by class discussion of these presentations and other material on current research methodology.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 200A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Graduate Colloquium for Economics III
description: Weekly reports and colloquia by faculty, students, and visitors. Supplemented by class discussion of these presentations and other material on current research methodology.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 200B with a minimum grade of B-

title: Mathematics for Economists
description: Gives students the mathematical background required for graduate work in economics. Topics covered include multivariate calculus, differential equations, and linear algebra.

title: Microeconomic Theory I
description: Theoretical microeconomics. Emphasis on the meaning and empirical interpretation of theoretical models. Topics include theory of the firm, theory of the market, theory of the consumer, duality theory, application to econometrics, general equilibrium and welfare economics, uncertainty, game theory.

title: Microeconomic Theory II
description: Theoretical microeconomics. Emphasis on the meaning and empirical interpretation of theoretical models. Topics include theory of the firm, theory of the market, theory of the consumer, duality theory, application to econometrics, general equilibrium and welfare economics, uncertainty, game theory.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Microeconomic Theory III
description: Theoretical microeconomics. Emphasis on the meaning and empirical interpretation of theoretical models. Topics include theory of the firm, theory of the market, theory of the consumer, duality theory, application to econometrics, general equilibrium and welfare economics, uncertainty, game theory.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210B with a minimum grade of B-

title: Macroeconomic Theory I
description: Advanced macroeconomic theory including alternative macroeconomic models, microeconomic foundations of macroeconomics, investment and growth theory, inflation and unemployment, rational expectations and macroeconomic policy, wealth effects, crowding out and fiscal policy, money and interest, open economy models.

title: Macroeconomic Theory II
description: Advanced macroeconomic theory including alternative macroeconomic models, microeconomic foundations of macroeconomics, investment and growth theory, inflation and unemployment, rational expectations and macroeconomic policy, wealth effects, crowding out and fiscal policy, money and interest, open economy models.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210D with a minimum grade of B-

title: Macroeconomic Theory III
description: Advanced macroeconomic theory including alternative macroeconomic models, microeconomic foundations of macroeconomics, investment and growth theory, inflation and unemployment, rational expectations and macroeconomic policy, wealth effects, crowding out and fiscal policy, money and interest, open economy models.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210E with a minimum grade of B-

title: Macroeconomics Theory II Lab
description: Overview of stochastic processes; introduction to dynamic programming; two equilibrium concepts; Ricardian equivalence; real business cycle model; complete versus incomplete markets; asset pricing and the equity premium puzzle.

title: Statistics and Econometrics I
description: Takes up where ECON 202 leaves off. Continuing in the likelihood perspective, begins with Bayesian point estimation and then covers interval estimation and hypothesis testing from both frequentist and Bayesian perspectives.

title: Statistics and Econometrics II
description: Begins by relaxing the ideal conditions of the standard regression model. Potential topics include kernel density estimation, instrumental variables (IV), two stage least squares (2SLS), panel data models, and simulation-based Bayesian methods, including Gibbs sampling, and the bootstrap.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 220A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Statistics and Econometrics III
description: Covers econometric time series, discrete choice and count models, sample selection, and duration models along with Bayesian and classical asymptotic methods.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 220B with a minimum grade of B-

title: Statistics and Econometrics Laboratory I
description: Discussion of problems in statistics and econometrics, and their relationships to statistical and econometrics theory. Instruction in the use of computers for applied econometric work.

title: Statistics and Econometrics Laboratory II
description: Discussion of problems in statistics and econometrics, and their relationships to statistical and econometrics theory. Instruction in the use of computers for applied econometric work.

title: Statistics and Econometrics Laboratory III
description: Discussion of problems in statistics and econometrics, and their relationships to statistical and econometrics theory. Instruction in the use of computers for applied econometric work.

title: Experimental Econ I
description: An introduction to experimental social science. Students learn experimental methodology, design, and analysis, and be exposed to active research areas. Each student writes a proposal for their own experiment and presents the design in class.

title: Experimental Econ II
description: Focuses on implementing experimental projects in a laboratory environment. Subjects learn about human subjects protection, program experimental software for their own projects, and conduct live experiment sessions.

title: Special Topics in Econometrics
description: Studies in selected areas of Econometrics. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
prerequisites_raw: Prerequisites vary

title: Business Cycles in Historical Perspective
description: Investigates business cycles in the United States and worldwide during the last two centuries. Topics include causes and consequences of business fluctuations, monetary and fiscal policy, models of fluctuations, and empirical macroeconomics.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210B with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210C with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210D with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210E with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210F with a minimum grade of B-

title: Health and Development in Historical Perspective
description: Investigates the evolution of population health over time and across the development process. Examines how the environment, nutrition, public health systems, and medical innovations have influenced health and demographic behavior. Also explores the interplay between health capital and economic growth.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210B with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210C with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 220A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 220B with a minimum grade of B-

title: Special Topics in Financial Economics
description: Studies in selected areas of Financial Economics. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
prerequisites_raw: Prerequisites vary

title: Industrial Organization I
description: Analysis of the structure and economic performance of markets, and the impact of public policy and their efficiency and equity. Effects of information structure. Oligopoly, cartels, mergers, vertical integration, patents, innovation, antitrust, and regulation.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 100B and ECON 203A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Industrial Organization II
description: Analysis of the structure and economic performance of markets, and the impact of public policy and their efficiency and equity. Effects of information structure. Price flexibility and dispersion, auctions, search and industrial structure, intrafirm organization.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 241A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 100B and ECON 203A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Development Economics
description: Uses theory and empirics to understand the economies of low- and middle-income countries. Explores the concept, determinants, and consequences of economic growth, drawing on historical and cross-country evidence. Topics include poverty, inequality, agriculture, demography, and strategies of risk management.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210B with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210C with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 220A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 220B with a minimum grade of B-

title: Game Theory
description: A formal introduction to non-cooperative game theory. Topics include properties of Nash Equilibrium and equilibrium refinements, games with imperfect information, and games with incomplete information.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210B with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210C with a minimum grade of B-

title: Advanced Game Theory
description: Provides advanced instruction in game theory. The topics covered will be (i) the theory of repeated games and (ii) evolutionary game theory. Applications include bargaining, collusion, reputation, social norms, and the evolution of preferences via natural selection and cultural transmission.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 243A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Empirical Methods in Applied Microeconomics
description: Focuses on the empirical methods used in modern applied microeconomics. Teaches methods that can be applied to produce original research in applied fields using cross-sectional and panel data. Applications will be drawn heavily from labor, public, health and development economics.

title: Special Topics in Microeconomics
description: Studies in selected areas of Microeconomics. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
prerequisites_raw: Prerequisites vary

title: Labor Economics I
description: Analysis of the relationships between education and the labor market (human capital theory), between resources devoted to education and the return to education (the education production function) and between education and labor market inequality (the theory of skill-biased technical change).
prerequisites_raw: ECON 203A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Labor Economics II
description: Analysis of core topics in labor economics, with an emphasis on empirical methods. Topics may include minimum wages, discrimination, gender, aging and retirement, labor market networks, personnel economics, and employment policy.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 203A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Microeconomics and Public Policy
description: Introduces the fundamental principles of microeconomics that are required for applied policy analysis. Provides students with an intuitive understanding of the microeconomic approach, and familiarizes them with concepts used in applied public policy analysis.

title: Special Topics in Labor Economics
description: Studies in selected areas of Labor Economics. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
prerequisites_raw: Prerequisites vary

title: Monetary Economics II
description: Surveys recent issues on monetary policy in uncertain environments. Examines settings where both the policy makers and the private sector are uncertain of future outcomes or the underlying economic structure.

title: International Trade I
description: Covers theoretical models, empirical methods, and policy issues in international trade. Following the conventional treatment of the Richardian model, the Heckscher-Ohlin model and the specific factors model, new trade models which incorporate scale economics and imperfect competition will be discussed.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210B with a minimum grade of B-

title: International Trade II
description: Covers theoretical models, empirical methods, and policy issues in international trade. Following the conventional treatment of the Richardian model, the Heckscher-Ohlin model, and the specific factors model, new trade models which incorporate scale economics and imperfect competition are discussed.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 261A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210B with a minimum grade of B-

title: Advanced Macroeconomics I
description: Students build Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) macroeconomic models from microeconomic foundations. This approach emphasizes intertemporal optimization by firms and households and typically incorporates nominal rigidities such as sluggish price and/or wage adjustment.

title: Special Topics in Macroeconomics
description: Studies in selected areas of Macroeconomics. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
prerequisites_raw: Prerequisites vary

title: Political Economy I
description: Political Economy lies at the intersection of economics and political science. Studies effects of politics on the economy and uses tools derived from economics to understand the behavior of governments and of citizens when they deal with politics.

title: Political Economy II
description: Political Economy lies at the intersection of economics and political science. Studies effects of politics on the economy and uses tools derived from economics to understand the behavior of governments and of citizens when they deal with politics.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 270A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Political Economy III
description: Political Economy lies at the intersection of economics and political science. Studies effects of politics on the economy and uses tools derived from economics to understand the behavior of governments and of citizens when they deal with politics.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 270B with a minimum grade of B-

title: Economics of Criminal Justice
description: Considers empirical research from the economics literature on various topics related to the criminal justice system, such as policing, bail reform, incarceration, or recidivism.

title: Public Economics I
description: Covers welfare economics, the theory of optimal taxation, tax incidence, and empirical methods in tax policy. Empirical topics include tax evasion, measurement of incidence, efficiency costs, and other policy issues.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210B with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210C with a minimum grade of B-

title: Public Economics II
description: Covers the theory of public goods and models of decentralized provision of such goods, including voluntary provision, voting, bureaucratic provision, and preference revelation mechanisms, as well as the Tiebout model. Also covers externalities, cost-benefit analysis, and intergovernmental competition.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210B with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210C with a minimum grade of B-

title: Public Economics III
description: Covers the rationale for and effects of government intervention in insurance markets and for redistribution. Includes theoretical and empirical analyses of cash and in-kind assistance programs, unemployment insurance, disability insurance, Social Security, and other programs.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210B with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210C with a minimum grade of B-

title: Economics of Government
description: Prepares students to analyze public policy questions with tools from economics. By the end, students should be able to identify important economic issues in public policy debates and consume and critique economic research on these topics.

title: Special Topics in Political Economy
description: Studies in selected areas of Political Economy. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
prerequisites_raw: Prerequisites vary

title: Urban Economics I
description: Economic reasons for the existence of cities, analysis of urban spatial structure, urban sprawl, Third World urbanization, hedonic price analysis, housing tenure choice.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Urban Economics II
description: Housing in the portfolio, land-use controls, rent control, homelessness, neighborhood effects, urban quality-of-life measurement, and subcenters.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Transportation Economics II
description: Economics of the airline industry. Hub-and-spoke networks, the effects of competition on airfares, price dispersion, airline alliances, airport congestion, product unbundling.
prerequisites_raw: ECON 282A with a minimum grade of B-

title: Health Economics
description: Introduction to graduate-level Health Economics. Research-oriented and focuses on the synthesis and critical examination of existing Economics research, as well as analyzing and producing research, with a focus on the U.S.
prerequisites_raw: ( ECON 210A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210B with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 210C with a minimum grade of B-) and ( ECON 220A with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 220B with a minimum grade of B- and ECON 220C with a minimum grade of B-) or UPPP 215 with a minimum grade of B- and UPPP 240 with a minimum grade of B-

title: Dissertation Research
description: Dissertation research with Economics faculty.

title: Cyber-Physical Systems Design
description: Requirements and specification, models of computation, tools, design, merging cyber and physical, data-driven modeling for edge artificial intelligence systems, cyber-physical examples. Design process, specification, requirements, modeling, components, selection, interfaces, system structure, different levels, verification, testing.

title: Embedded Systems Modeling and Design
description: Embedded systems definition, system-level specification, models and languages. Concepts, requirements, examples. Embedded system models at different levels of abstraction. Test benches, design under test, IP components. Discrete event simulation, semantics, and algorithms.

title: Embedded System Software
description: Embedded system software requirements, concepts, and examples for applications in the cyber-physical domain. Embedded operating systems, real-time system software (RTOS), I/O software. Multithreading. System software for power and energy management, and middleware.

title: Sensors, Actuators, and Sensor Networks
description: Fundamental principles and applications of sensors, actuators. Smart sensors and microsensor/microactuator array devices. Introduction to signal processing and sensor/actuator networks, deployment and architecture, wireless communication, multiple access control layer, data gathering, routing and querying, collaborating signal processing.

title: Security and Privacy in Cyber-Physical Systems
description: Embedded and cyber-physical systems security: attacks and countermeasures, authentication, identification, confidentiality, data integrity, authorization, access control, security protocols. Privacy awareness and mitigation. Side-channel attacks and defenses. Applications of public key and symmetric cryptography, digital certificates, credentials.

title: Control Systems for Cyber-Physical Systems
description: Dynamic models, from first principles or via identification. Concepts in control (stability, controllability, observability). Control design (continuous times) and digital implementation. Introduction to optimization and direct discrete time control. Multi-agent systems, their control and implementation related concepts.

title: Cyber-Physical Systems Case Studies
description: Covers CPS case studies in applications such as (but not limited to): automotive and transportation, manufacturing, power distribution grid, medical and healthcare, robotics, civil infrastructure, avionics.

title: Cyber-Physical Systems Project
description: Students are required to complete a project that deals with a specific emphasis of Cyber-Physical Systems, such as (but not limited to): automotive, transportation, manufacturing, power grid, medical healthcare, robotics, civil infrastructure, avionics.
prerequisites_raw: ECPS 202 with a minimum grade of B- or ECPS 203 with a minimum grade of B- or ECPS 216 with a minimum grade of B-

title: Machine Learning and Data Mining
description: Introduction to principles of machine learning and data-mining. Learning algorithms for classifications, regression, and clustering. Emphasis is on discriminative classification methods such as decision trees, rules, nearest neighbor, linear models, and naive Bayes.

title: Entrepreneurship for Scientists and Engineers
description: Real-world introduction to the theory and practice of entrepreneurship. Explores organizational, strategic, and financial challenges; start-up strategies; business-idea evaluation; and business-plan writing. Presentations by prestigious entrepreneurs and industry leaders.

title: Foundations of Autonomous Systems
description: Introduces the fundamentals of perception, planning, and control of autonomous systems. Students learn how to use Robotic Operating Systems (ROS), integrate data from various sensors while implementing algorithms for localization, planning, mapping, and control of autonomous vehicles.

title: Internet of Things Systems and Software
description: Internet of Things (IoT) concept, sensors and actuators, serial protocols, network and communication protocols and programming, IoT platforms, real-time performance, middleware architecture for IoT, edge and cloud support for IoT applications.

title: Preparation for Capstone Design
description: Provides students in the Master of Embedded and Cyber Physical Systems program with information, practical skills, and preparation for their capstone project. Students form capstone teams and participate in initial project matching with faculty and industry mentors.

title: Internship
description: Students go through practical training under an industry mentor in a technical field corresponding to their area of interest.

title: MECPS Proseminar
description: Information and practical skills for students in the MECPS program. Also covers professional development career planning.

title: Special Topics in CPS
description: Studies in selected areas of CPS. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

title: Introduction to Electrical Engineering and Computer Engineering
description: Introduction to the fields of Electrical Engineering and Computer Engineering, including possible careers in both traditional and new emerging areas. Background on both the Electrical Engineering and the Computer Engineering majors, curriculum requirements, specializations, and faculty research interests.

title: Computational Methods in Electrical and Computer Engineering
description: An introduction to computers and structured programming. Binary Data Representation. Hands-on experience with a high-level structured programming language. Introduction to algorithm efficiency. Applications of structured programming in solving engineering problems. Programming laboratory.
prerequisites_raw: MATH 2A or AP Calculus AB with a minimum score of 3

title: Introduction to Programming
description: An introduction to computers and programming. Python programming syntax/style, types. Numbers and sequences. Control flow. I/O and errors/exceptions. Function calling, parameter passing, formal arguments, return values. Variable scoping. Programming laboratory.
prerequisites_raw: MATH 2A or AP Calculus AB with a minimum score of 3

title: Computer Systems and C Programming
description: Introduction to computing systems. Data representation and operations. Simple logic design. Basic computer organization. Instruction set architecture and assembly language programming. Introduction to C. Functions and recursion, data structures, pointers. Programming laboratory.
prerequisites_raw: EECS 12

title: Advanced C Programming
description: C language programming concepts. Control flow, function calls, recursion. Basic and composite data types, static and dynamic data structures. Program modules and compilation units. Preprocessor macros. C standard libraries.
prerequisites_raw: EECS 10 or EECS 20

title: Software Engineering Project in C Language
description: Hands-on experience with the ANSI-C programming language. Medium-sized programming projects, team work. Software specification, documentation, implementation, testing. Definition of data structures and application programming interface. Creation of program modules, linking with external libraries. Rule-based compilation, version control.
prerequisites_raw: EECS 22

title: Introduction to Digital Systems
description: Digital representation of information. Specification, analysis, design and optimization or combinational and sequential logic, register-transfer components and register-transfer systems with datapaths and controllers. Introduction to high-level and algorithmic state-machines and custom processors.
prerequisites_raw: I&C SCI 31 or EECS 10 or EECS 12 or ENGRMAE 10 or I&C SCI 32A
